title: Modules and the Standard Library
summary: Use import to bring in math, datetime and random, and import a module you wrote yourself (number_tools) from another program. Practice with circle area and hypotenuse, a date countdown, lotto numbers and a number-guessing game.

math_practice.summary: Practice 1. Read a radius and print the circle's area and circumference, then read two legs and print the hypotenuse. math.pi and math.hypot, loaded with import math, are reached with the dot (.).
math_practice.notes: The NameError in the fifth step is on purpose. In the actual practice, fill in the TODOs with nano math_practice.py, then rerun the first step and compare its output with the finished version.
steps: Runs the program with the inputs 3, 3, 4 fed in ahead of time (you can also run python3 math_practice.py yourself and type them). The starter only has TODOs, so the prompts Radius: First leg: Second leg: come out run together on one line with no results. Piped input is not echoed to the screen, which is why the prompts look glued together.
The finished version prints Area: 28.27, Circumference: 18.85, Hypotenuse: 5.0. round(..., 2) keeps two decimal places.
Second test: with radius 1 the area is 3.14 (equal to π) and the circumference is 6.28. The hypotenuse of 5 and 12 is 13.0.
Checks the math functions from the slides in one go: 2 3 120 6 5.0. Floor, ceil, factorial, greatest common divisor and hypotenuse.
Using sqrt without importing it gives NameError: name 'sqrt' is not defined. Read the traceback from the last line.
from math import sqrt, pi brings the names in directly, so you can use them without a prefix: 4.0 and 3.141592653589793.

date_check.summary: Practice 2. Read a date in YYYY-MM-DD format, turn it into a date with datetime.strptime, and print its weekday name (strftime("%A")) and the number of days remaining from today (date.today()).
steps: The starter only reads the date and converts it, so it prints nothing apart from the prompt. The date is well formed, so there is no error either.
This is today's date as the virtual machine sees it. The days remaining below are counted from this date.
Christmas 2026 is a Friday. The Days remaining value depends on today's date.
Feeding in today's date gives Days remaining: 0.
A date that has already passed gives a negative number of days remaining. 2026-01-01 is a Thursday.
Date arithmetic from the slides: the difference of two dates is a timedelta whose .days is 47, and the date + 100 days is 2027-01-05.

number_tools.summary: Lab 1. number_tools.py is a module holding the functions average and count_above, and stats_report.py in the same folder calls them through import number_tools to print a score report. The if __name__ == "__main__": block at the bottom of the module shows a demo only when the file is run directly.
number_tools.notes: The ZeroDivisionError in the last step is shown on purpose. After filling in the two TODO functions, rerun the first two steps: you should get Demo average: 5.0, Average: 88.0, Above 85: 3, the same as the finished version.
steps: When run directly, __name__ is "__main__", so the demo runs. The starter's average is just pass and returns None, so it prints Demo average: None.
The starter report prints only Scores: [88, 92, 79, 93]. import number_tools passes silently: the demo does not run when the module is imported.
Running the finished module directly: Demo average: 5.0 (2+4+6+8 divided by 4).
Finished report: Average: 88.0 (352 / 4), Above 85: 3 (88, 92, 93). The script's own folder comes first in the module search path, so the number_tools in the solutions folder is the one imported.
Inside an imported module, __name__ is the file name minus .py: number_tools. That is why the demo line is not printed.

The average of an empty list divides by zero and raises ZeroDivisionError: division by zero (Lab 1 Checks). How to handle this error is next session's topic. Because the cd happens inside the parentheses, the current folder does not change.

lotto.summary: Lab 2. Read the number of games (1–5); for each game draw 6 different numbers with random.sample(range(1, 46), 6), sort them and print them on one line. Input outside the range prints Invalid games.
steps: The starter's loop body is pass, so even with 3 as input not a single line of numbers is printed.
The finished version prints three lines. Check that each line is sorted smallest first, has no duplicates and stays between 1 and 45. The numbers change on every run.
Input 1 gives exactly one line. print(*numbers) unpacks the list and prints it separated by spaces, without brackets or commas.
6 and 0 are both out of range, so only Invalid games is printed.
With seed(42) the same sequence comes back: 82 15, and then 82 again. seed is useful for testing, but we do not use it for the lotto.

guessing.summary: Lab 3 (take-home). The computer picks a secret number from 1 to 100 once, answers each guess with Higher/Lower until it is guessed, and on success prints Correct! with the number of attempts and ends the loop with break.
guessing.notes: The EOFError in the first step is an intended error showing that the starter never finishes. To play yourself, run python3 ../../solutions/session1/guessing.py, start at 50 and halve the range according to Higher/Lower (you can always win within 7 guesses). The starter's TODO is to split Higher, Lower and Correct! with if/elif/else and break on a correct guess. When you are done, check with seq 1 100 | python3 guessing.py | tail -n 3 that the last lines match the finished version.
steps: The starter has neither the comparison nor break, so while True never ends. It uses up the three input lines and the fourth input() raises EOFError: EOF when reading a line. If you ran it yourself, you would have to stop it with Ctrl+C.
Feeding 1 to 100 in order into the finished version prints Higher until it reaches the secret, then ends with Correct! Attempts: N. Here N is the secret itself. Only the last three lines are shown.
Feeding the numbers backwards from 100 prints Lower this time. A new secret is chosen on every run.
